Configuration Management

1. Configuration Management

One correctly configured server is a useful result. Ten servers maintained by memory and improvised commands are an emerging reliability problem. HarborWorks needs a reviewable description of desired state, a controlled application process, and evidence that the resulting service actually meets its requirements.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch029.xhtml — Chapter 27 — Configuration Management

2. Converge to declared state twice

Idempotency means a repeated accepted configuration does not make unnecessary changes; validate the application after convergence. A script appends the same configuration line each time it runs.

SOURCE: Converge to declared state twice

3. Chapter 27 — Configuration Management

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch029.xhtml — Chapter 27 — Configuration Management

4. 27.1 The Problem with Manual Administration

Manual changes are easy to make and hard to reproduce. Two administrators can solve the same immediate problem differently, leaving inconsistent paths, permissions, packages, or restart behavior. An undocumented emergency repair can disappear during the next rebuild.

The answer is not to prohibit investigation. Operators still need to inspect and sometimes intervene. The requirement is to reconcile accepted changes into the declared configuration and preserve a change record. Temporary exceptions should have an owner and expiry.

Ask whether a new machine can be built from the record without relying on one person’s recollection. If not, the existing machine is carrying undocumented knowledge that becomes a recovery dependency.

Linux example — 27.1

Demonstrate reproducible state under your own account.

What to check: Repeatable commands are a start; a managed baseline must also describe owner, mode, and contents.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch029.xhtml — 27.1 The Problem with Manual Administration

6. 27.2 Infrastructure as Code

Infrastructure as code stores intended infrastructure and configuration in reviewable files and applies them through controlled tooling. It enables versioning, comparison, testing, and repeatable changes. It does not make every file in a repository correct or every deployment safe.

Separate provisioning from configuration. One tool may create a VM and network, while another installs packages and manages service files. Define their boundaries so two systems do not independently overwrite the same property.

Keep secrets out of ordinary source control. A configuration repository should refer to a protected secret source rather than becoming a permanent record of passwords. Removing a secret in a later commit does not erase its earlier disclosure.

Linux example — 27.2

Save a declarative local specification.

What to check: This worksheet describes intent; it is not itself an executable Ansible playbook.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch029.xhtml — 27.2 Infrastructure as Code

8. 27.3 Desired State

Desired state says what should be true: a package is installed, a directory has specified ownership, a file contains approved content, or a service is enabled. The tool compares observed state with that target and applies relevant changes.

This differs from blindly rerunning a history of commands. echo setting >> file describes an action that adds another line each time; a managed template describes the complete intended file. The latter is easier to compare and recover.

State also needs scope. A role managing one NGINX fragment should not overwrite every unrelated site. Explicitly assign ownership of directories, files, and settings to avoid accidental competition between teams.

Linux example — 27.3

Compare intended mode with observed mode.

What to check: The observed 750 mode can be checked against an explicit desired value.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch029.xhtml — 27.3 Desired State

10. 27.4 Idempotency

An idempotent configuration converges without unnecessary further changes when reapplied to a system already in the intended state. It should not duplicate users, append repeated lines, or restart a service on every run without a reason.

Idempotency is not a synonym for safe or correct. A playbook that consistently writes the wrong firewall policy is still wrong. Test first-run behavior, second-run stability, failure handling, and the actual application contract.

Some operations are inherently event-like, such as a schema migration or certificate revocation. Represent them with explicit prerequisites, state checks, and approval rather than pretending that every operation can be made safe by adding an unless condition.

Linux example — 27.4

Repeat a convergent local operation.

What to check: Repetition retains the intended directory and mode without duplicate objects.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch029.xhtml — 27.4 Idempotency

12. 27.5 Ansible Architecture

Ansible commonly runs from a control node, connects to managed Linux hosts over SSH, and executes modules, often with a Python interpreter on the managed host. There are exceptions and specialized connection methods, so verify prerequisites for the modules in use.

The control node holds inventory, playbooks, dependencies, and access to credentials. Protect it as a management plane. Do not disable SSH host-key checking to remove the inconvenience of onboarding new hosts; establish trust through the approved provisioning process.

Pin or otherwise control the Ansible version and required collections in a reproducible environment. Newer documentation may describe options absent from a distribution package. Record ansible --version and collection versions with the tested automation. (R58)

Linux example — 27.5

Inspect the installed Ansible environment.

What to check: Controller Python, configuration path, and module search paths influence execution.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch029.xhtml — 27.5 Ansible Architecture

14. 27.6 Inventories

An inventory identifies hosts and groups, and can associate variables with them. Group by operational role and environment, not only by naming convention. Separate lab and production inventories to make the target boundary visible.

An illustrative INI inventory is:

Replace the address and account with verified values. Do not store passwords in this file. Use ansible-inventory -i inventory.ini --graph to inspect grouping before a change, and a host-listing option on the intended play to confirm the execution target.

An empty or unexpectedly broad group must stop the workflow. A correct playbook aimed at the wrong hosts is still an incident.

Linux example — 27.6

Create a localhost-only inventory and validate its interpretation.

What to check: This inventory targets only the controller; do not substitute a production inventory casually.

17. 27.7 Ad Hoc Commands

Ad hoc commands run a module against an inventory selection without a full playbook. They are useful for bounded inspection and simple verified operations.

Ansible’s ping module checks connection and module execution prerequisites; it is not ICMP ping. A successful result does not prove that the web service is healthy.

Use modules rather than shell syntax when possible. The command module does not interpret pipes and shell expansion like a shell. That is often a safety advantage. Choose the shell module only when shell behavior is genuinely required and inputs are controlled.

Linux example — 27.7

Run an ad hoc localhost connectivity check.

What to check: Ansible ping tests module execution and Python availability; it is not ICMP ping.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch029.xhtml — 27.7 Ad Hoc Commands

20. 27.8 Playbooks

A playbook is a YAML description of plays and tasks directed at selected hosts. Read it as a program: it has inputs, branching, effects, failure behavior, and dependencies. Indentation and types matter.

Use fully qualified module names, descriptive task names, and explicit ownership and modes. Quoting a mode such as '0644' avoids ambiguous numeric interpretation in YAML-related tooling.

Begin with syntax validation and a small target. Check mode predicts changes for modules that support it, but it cannot prove the full runtime behavior of every task or dependency. Diff mode can expose sensitive file content, so use it selectively. (R58)

Linux example — 27.8

Write a playbook that changes only a fresh local lab directory.

What to check: Syntax validation precedes --check and a real local run; no root privilege is requested.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch029.xhtml — 27.8 Playbooks

22. 27.9 Variables

Variables adapt a shared implementation to hosts or environments. Examples include a content path, service name, or approved release marker. Document defaults and required values; do not rely on a surprising precedence chain to communicate intent.

Validate values that influence paths, host selection, privileges, or network exposure. A typo in a content marker is different from a variable changing /srv/harbor/site to /. The latter needs explicit constraints, not a more enthusiastic recursive task.

Avoid excessive configurability. A role with dozens of loosely related switches can be harder to reason about than two clear roles. Expose decisions that actually vary while keeping security and ownership invariants deliberate.

Linux example — 27.9

Override a variable in a controlled invocation.

What to check: Extra variables have high precedence; avoid using them to bypass reviewed production settings.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch029.xhtml — 27.9 Variables

24. 27.10 Templates

Templates combine reviewed structure with selected variables to produce configuration files. Ansible’s template module uses Jinja2 and can validate a candidate before replacing the destination. The validation command receives the temporary file through %s; it does not automatically run as a shell pipeline.

A validation command must match the file’s grammar and context. nginx -t -c %s validates a complete top-level configuration, not an isolated server fragment that belongs inside http. For fragments, use a reviewed wrapper or stage and validate the complete assembled configuration.

File-level atomic replacement is useful but does not make a multi-file rollout transactional. Backups, service reloads, and rollback still need coordination. Protect template output containing secrets and avoid leaking it through diffs. (R58)

Linux example — 27.10

Write a small Jinja template candidate.

What to check: Rendering requires defined variables and the Ansible template module in a reviewed playbook.

Template task candidate

Add this task to the localhost-only playbook after defining course_environment and creating report.j2. Review the diff, run twice, and expect no second-run change unless the rendered values differ.

27. 27.11 Roles

A role organizes related tasks, handlers, defaults, templates, and files into a reusable unit. A good role owns a coherent responsibility with clear inputs and outputs. For HarborWorks, base account policy and a static website might be separate roles.

Handlers perform deferred operations in response to change notifications. A configuration task can notify a reload handler so an unchanged run avoids unnecessary reloads. Understand handler timing and failure behavior; notifications do not guarantee that a handler will execute under every later failure condition.

Test roles on supported distributions. A package-name variable alone does not cover differences in service names, security frameworks, configuration includes, or default identities. Keep those differences visible in tasks and validation.

Linux example — 27.11

Inspect role tooling without installing external content.

What to check: Review role sources and pin versions before installing or applying them.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch029.xhtml — 27.11 Roles

29. 27.12 Secrets

Ansible Vault can encrypt selected stored data, but decrypted values can still appear during execution, templating, logs, or debugging unless those paths are protected. Encryption at rest is one boundary, not the whole secret lifecycle.

Use no_log on tasks that would disclose sensitive values, protect temporary files and controller access, and limit the final destination’s permissions. Prefer short-lived credentials and an approved secret-management integration where available.

Design recovery and rotation. A fleet cannot be rebuilt if its only decryption credential existed on the lost controller. Conversely, distributing a permanent controller-wide secret to every managed host expands the compromise boundary unnecessarily.

Linux example — 27.12

Create a new encrypted lab vault file.

What to check: The tool prompts for a vault password and opens an editor; keep actual credentials out of examples and command arguments.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch029.xhtml — 27.12 Secrets

31. 27.13 Automating Server Configuration

Build automation in small, verifiable layers: inventory and connectivity, packages, identity, directories, content, service configuration, activation, and application checks. Validate prerequisites before destructive or access-changing operations.

Keep the administration path separate from application deployment. A content update should not also rewrite SSH policy merely because both belong somewhere in a broad “server setup” playbook. Separate change scopes reduce rollback complexity.

Run the play twice on a disposable server and inspect what changes the second time. Then deliberately introduce one bounded drift and confirm the tool repairs only that owned state. Add a client-visible acceptance check to detect a configuration that is syntactically valid but behaviorally wrong.

Linux example — 27.13

Preview the localhost playbook from section 27.8.

What to check: Check mode support varies by module; diff can expose secrets if used on sensitive files.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch029.xhtml — 27.13 Automating Server Configuration

33. 27.14 Managing Fleets of Linux Servers

Fleet changes need staged rollout, stop conditions, and failure-domain awareness. serial can limit the number of hosts processed in a batch, but it does not automatically drain a load balancer or prove remaining capacity.

Start with a representative canary, observe agreed metrics, then expand. Define who can halt the rollout and how failed or unreachable hosts are tracked. Unreachable is not equivalent to compliant or successfully skipped.

Maintain a record of desired revision and observed state per host. Emergency changes should be reconciled, not overwritten blindly during the next scheduled run. Configuration management becomes reliable when it includes operational decisions rather than only fast execution.

Linux example — 27.14

Create a fresh localhost inventory and preview the intended host scope.

What to check: Only localhost should appear. For a fleet playbook, inspect --list-hosts with its reviewed inventory before execution.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch029.xhtml — 27.14 Managing Fleets of Linux Servers

35. Requirement

Use a complete Ansible playbook to create one teaching directory and one status file under the current user’s home. Repeated execution must preserve the same content without duplication. This unprivileged exercise teaches convergence before expanding automation to remote root access.

Install Ansible through an approved environment, then save the following as site.yml. This play intentionally uses localhost, a local connection, and no privilege escalation:

The path assertion is a teaching guard, not a defense against a malicious local filesystem. Use a trusted home directory and run as an ordinary user. Do not execute this with sudo.

37. Validate, apply, and repeat

Check mode may report prospective directory and file changes, but its predictions are not a substitute for the first real run. On the second actual run, already-correct managed tasks should report no change. That is an expected result to inspect, not a claimed execution on every Ansible version.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch029.xhtml — Validate, apply, and repeat

38. Validate, apply, and repeat · example 1

Check mode may report prospective directory and file changes, but its predictions are not a substitute for the first real run. On the second actual run, already-correct managed tasks should report no change. That is an expected result to inspect, not a claimed execution on every Ansible version.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch029.xhtml — Validate, apply, and repeat

39. Bounded drift and recovery

Modify only the fixture’s status file manually, then rerun the play. It should restore the declared content. Try an invalid site_state through an explicit extra variable; the assertion should stop before the managed change. Restore the valid input afterward.

The simplest alternative—appending a status line through a shell task—would accumulate lines. The managed file replaces that history with a complete intended state. In production, apply the same discipline to a reviewed remote inventory with least-privilege access and service-specific validation.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch029.xhtml — Bounded drift and recovery

40. Practice and implementation lab

Extend the fixture to use a template with a release marker and add a content assertion after deployment. Do not put the current timestamp into the managed file unless a change on every run is truly intended. Design a canary rollout for three hypothetical web servers and name its explicit stop conditions.

Check your understanding. Does Ansible ping test ICMP? No. Does check mode prove every task will work? No. Can an idempotent playbook still be dangerous? Yes, when its desired state or target is wrong.

Chapter takeaway. Configuration management turns operational intent into reviewed, testable state—not merely commands executed at greater speed.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch029.xhtml — Practice and implementation lab

41. Converge without repeated changes

Exit 10 is this fixture's change indicator, not an Ansible exit-code convention. The solution checks the stated outcome explicitly. These fixture results do not establish that a real privileged service is configured correctly.

SOURCE: Converge without repeated changes
